#7642. Court to hear argument on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for violations of the Constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Monday, Nov. 9, in a lawsuit brought by a Hawaii man, Kekai Watanabe, who contends that a prison paramedic violated his constitutional rights when he failed to provide medical treatment after Watanabe was injured during a fight while in federal custody. Both the paramedic, Francis Nielsen, and the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Nielsen, urge the justices to shut down Watanabe’s case; Nielsen also suggests that the court should go even further and foreclose efforts to recover from federal officials for violations of the Constitution.

More than 50 years ago, in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the Supreme Court ruled that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages.

In the years that followed, the justices have extended their decision in Bivens only twice. In Davis v. Passman, in 1979, the court held that a former congressional staffer could sue a member of Congress for alleged sex discrimination in violation of the Fifth Amendment. And in Carlson v. Green, the court held that the estate of an inmate, who died after having an asthma attack, could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

But since then the court has resisted efforts to rely on Bivens. Four years ago, in Egbert v. Boule, it observed that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.” Moreover, Justice Clarence Thomas noted for the majority “that if we were called to decide Bivens today, we would decline to discover any implied causes of action in the Constitution. But,” Thomas wrote, “to decide the case before us, we need not reconsider Bivens itself.”

In the present case, Watanabe was badly injured during a gang-related fight while at a federal detention center in Hawaii. He contends that he told Nielsen, who treated him, that his pain was a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, but Nielsen gave him only over-the-counter pain medication. Watanabe alleges that he was kept in solitary confinement for more than two months, during which he did not see a specialist or go to a hospital. When Watanabe eventually obtained an x-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

In February 2022, Watanabe went to federal court in Honolulu. Relying on Bivens and Carlson, he alleged that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment because Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim arose in a new context – that is, it was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case for his claim to go forward.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but in its view “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Nielsen appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

In his brief on the merits, Nielsen contends that Watanabe’s case fails both prongs of the “demanding two-part test” that the Supreme Court has established for Bivens claims. That test, he adds, boils down to “whether there is any reason to think Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy.”

The first question is whether the claim arises in a new context from the three cases in which it has recognized Bivens claims. “Even ‘small’ differences from the original Bivens trio” of cases “will present a new context,” Nielsen writes: “‘a modest extension is still an extension.’” Watanabe’s claim, Nielsen argues, is not modest but is instead “meaningfully—profoundly—different” from Carlson. As an initial matter, he says, the facts are markedly dissimilar, because the inmate in Carlson died just hours after the attack, so that monetary compensation for his estate was the only possible remedy. By contrast, Nielsen asserts, Watanabe’s “injury was neither fatal nor life-threatening,” and instead of monetary damages he could have sought more treatment or a move to a hospital through either internal prison appeals or by filing a lawsuit in court.

If the context is new, Nielsen continues, the next question is whether “there are ‘special factors’ indicating that” courts are “at least arguably less equipped than Congress to ‘weigh the costs and benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed.’ ‘If there is even a single “reason to pause before applying Bivens in a new context,” a court may not recognize a Bivens remedy.’” Nielsen points to at least two “special factors” at play in this case that “‘suggest[] that Congress did [not] want’” prisoners to be able to recover monetary compensation from federal officials. First, he said, the Administrative Remedy Program – a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979 – “provides an alternative remedial structure for federal prisoners.” Second, he added, the Prison Litigation Reform Act, enacted in 1996, requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Nielsen further tells the justices that they should throw out not only Watanabe’s claim but Bivens along with it. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson, he says, “are relics of the bygone days when federal courts thought it appropriate to create causes of action congress had not authorized.”

The federal government sides with Nielsen to the extent that he argues that Watanabe’s claim should be thrown out. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the court that “Carlson has become entirely obsolete” in light of new laws like the PLRA and the creation of the ARP. “And given courts’ lack of authority and expertise in setting prison policy,” Sauer said, “courts will always have a reason to pause before extending Carlson to that new context. That means that no more Carlson claims will be viable.” But, Sauer continues, the court should decline Nielsen’s suggestion to “consider overruling Bivens in this case. If the Court wishes to consider that question,” Sauer writes, “it should do so in the context of a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself.”

In his brief, Watanabe insists that his case “arises in th[e] prototypical Carlson context.” “It is,” he writes, “a damages action against a federal prison officer who was deliberately indifferent to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth Amendment.” Moreover, he continues, both his claim and the claim in Carlson involved “the same kind of defendant in the same kind of federal institution under the same legal framework.” The fact that he suffered from a different medical problem than Carlson, or that the inmate in Carlson died while Watanabe survived does not make his case a “new context,” he argues. Instead, he contends, such differences “are case-specific, factual variations to which” Carlson’s “settled rule applies.”

Watanabe pushes back against Nielsen’s contention that, because he is still alive, he (unlike the inmate in Carlson) also has other remedies available to him. Only money, he says, can compensate him for “his past pain and suffering.”

Watanabe tells the justices that, contrary to Nielsen’s suggestion, Congress has indicated that claims like his and the one in Carlson should be allowed to go forward, albeit with some restrictions. He points first to the Westfall Act, a 1988 law that stripped prisoners of their ability to sue federal officers under state law for their injuries, but specifically carved out an exception for “federal constitutional claims like those in Carlson.” And although the Prison Litigation Reform Act requires prisoners to pursue all of their internal appeals “before pursuing a Carlson claim,” it nonetheless shows, Watanabe argues, that Congress intended for Carlson claims to be available.

Watanabe urges the justices to leave Carlson in place even if the court might reach a different decision today. Among other things, he argues, that decision “was not egregiously wrong” and Congress has relied on it in fashioning remedies for inmates – two factors that courts consider when deciding whether to overturn their prior cases. And more broadly, he contends, if the Supreme Court were to overrule Carlson, it “would create a novel situation, never contemplated by Congress, in which federal prisoners who are subjected to needless suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment have no recourse against the responsible officers.”

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7640. Judge orders Albertsons to pay Washington $900 million over role in opioid crisis

The pharmacy chain put profits over the safety of patients, the state court determined.

SEATTLE (CN) â A Washington judge on Thursday ordered Albertsons to pay a whopping $900 million judgment after finding the grocery pharmacy chain neglected to guard against the misuse and diversion of addictive medications.

âThe state of Washington is in the throes of an opioid epidemic that is so wide-reaching and damaging that it has impacted Washingtonians throughout the state,â wrote King County Superior Court Judge Janet Helson in a 219-page opinion. âBased on the evidence presented at trial, the court finds that defendants Albertsons Companies, Inc. and Safeway, Inc. substantially contributed to the creation and maintenance of this public nuisance, and that the same yearslong unfair acts or practices that contributed to the nuisance also violated Washingtonâs Consumer Protection Act.â

The judgment follows a nine-week bench trial in which the state presented evidence of Albertsons failing to investigate or report shipments of significant quantities of suspicious orders of opioids into their own pharmacies.

The evidence also showed Albertsons had improper safeguards that led to diversion â transfer of prescription opioids to the black market â and failed to conduct due diligence when dispensing staggering quantities of opioid prescriptions that raised red flags of diversion.

âThe opioid crisis has been an equal opportunity monster, bringing its destruction not only to urban areas, but to many small towns and rural areas throughout our state,â Helson wrote. âThis ongoing crisis has affected, and interfered with, public health, public safety, public spaces, and the day-to-day life of Washington residents to the point that any efforts to remedy it will necessarily be massive in size, scope, and time.â

Albertsons acts as both a distributor and dispenser of prescription opioids and is required by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Controlled Substances Act to provide effective controls against diversion. Helson found the national pharmacy chain failed to do so.

âThe preponderance of evidence demonstrates that Albertsons never implemented and enforced policies or procedures that were effective at preventing the shipping of suspicious orders of prescription opioids to their stores, or the dispensing of âred flagâ prescriptions from those stores, without the required due diligence,â Helson wrote. âMoreover, Albertsons possessed, but routinely disregarded or ignored, information and tools that could have helped prevent diversion, choosing sales and profits over patient safety.â

The state presented evidence showing instances where tens of thousands of opioid pills were either diverted or inappropriately dispensed. Helson found the disregard for the health and safety of Washingtonians substantially contributed to the ongoing opioid crisis in the state.

Albertsons owns and operates more than 200 pharmacies in the state.

The court also found Albertsons repeatedly violated the Controlled Substances Act by dispensing and distributing addictive painkillers to increase its profits. The state presented evidence showing the pharmacy filled red-flagged prescriptions more than 6.5 million times without documenting its efforts to make sure the prescriptions were legitimate.

In a footnote, Helson acknowledged that many factors have contributed to the opioid epidemic â manufacturers misleading the public and medical community, well-intentioned state policies and medical community guidance regarding the need to treat pain, incompetent prescribers â but wrote that the existence of other factors, even substantial factors, does not excuse Albertsonsâ conduct.

Helson found Albertsons didnât properly staff its pharmacies, nor properly train the pharmacists on dispensing controlled substances. Nor did the pharmacy establish an adequate compliance department, putting company profit over patient safety, Helson determined.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown celebrated the courtâs ruling.

âThis is a victory for the people of Washington. When giant corporations put profits above safety, they will be held accountable,â Brown said in a statement. âThis verdict canât undo the devastating harms of the opioid crisis, but it will provide desperately needed resources to support treatment and prevent future crises.â

An expert witness testified that more than 19,000 state residents died from opioid-related overdoses between 1999 and 2023. During that time, the death rate nearly quadrupled from 3.5 to 36.2 per 100,000.

Over the last three years, 7,400 Washingtonians have died from opioid overdoses.

The stateâs evidence illustrated how Washingtonâs opioid crisis has decreased public safety, increased criminal justice costs and strained local government and law enforcement, Helson wrote. It also showed how the crisis has impacted public spaces, with a rise in homelessness, public drug use and litter of used needles and drug paraphernalia.

The state said the $900 million will help expand treatment and prevention resources.

A spokesperson for Albertsons said the company is disappointed by the court’s ruling, disagrees with its conclusions and is considering appealing.

âWe are proud of our pharmacists and their dedication to the patients and communities they serve, and we will continue to support our customers and communities across Washington through responsible pharmacy operations,â the spokesperson said.

#7637. Trio charged with impersonating CEOs using AI to steal millions from top companies

Feds say the three men stole more than $129 million in total, including more than $11.5 million from a single fintech company in the United Kingdom.

MANHATTAN (CN) â Three men used artificial intelligence to âimpersonate the voices and/or imagesâ of CEOs and bilk millions from their companies, according to an indictment unsealed Thursday in the Southern District of New York.

Federal prosecutors say Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit stole more than $129 million in total between 2024 and 2026 by pretending to be at least seven different high-profile corporate executives around the world.

According to prosecutors, the men targeted employees who were in a high enough position to authorize large wire transfers on behalf of their companies. Once the defendants identified their victim, the trio reportedly convinced their target that their help was needed on a confidential financial transaction â often a corporate acquisition.

Prosecutors say the men then invited the employees to a voice or video call, where using AI, they were able to swindle their target into believing they were actually the chief executives of the company.

âOn those calls, the defendants and their co-conspirators would use AI to mimic the voice and at times the image of the impersonated CEO in order to convince the victim employee that the transaction was real,â prosecutors claim.

Soall, Hazan and Sheetrit are accused of then passing the victim off to an attorney, who in reality, was once again just one of the men using AI to impersonate a real attorney at a major law firm.

âThe impersonated attorney would ultimately direct the victim employee to wire a large sum of money in furtherance of that financial transaction to a particular bank account, which was in fact controlled by members of the conspiracy,â prosecutors say. âIn sum, the purported corporate transactions were a sham, and the victim employees were not communicating with the real CEO or the real attorney.â

Itâs not immediately clear which companies were targeted by the novel heist, nor which law firms were impersonated to make it happen. But prosecutors say the men stole massive sums of money with each successful scam.

For instance, the government claims that, in March 2025, the men defrauded a United Kingdom-based fintech firm out of more than $11.5 million. In April 2025, they reportedly defrauded a Massachusetts-based mutual fund company out of more than $4.6 million. And in June 2025, they are accused of stealing more than $5.2 million from a Florida-based pet food company.

âAs alleged, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit abused groundbreaking super intelligence technology to impersonate real people and deceive corporate executives into sending them and their co-conspirators approximately $129 million,â said Jamie McDonald, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, using President Donald Trumpâs preferred term for artificial intelligence. âI encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime.â

Prosecutors say each man had a different role. Soall, a 41-year-old of Spain and the United Kingdom, used a handwritten script filled with lawyerly vocabulary to impersonate attorneys. Hazan, a 54-year old of Israel, and Sheetrit, a 42-year-old of Israel and the United Arab Emirates, laundered the stolen cash â prosecutors say that Hazan boasted that, when it comes to professional money laundering, he was ânumber one all over the world.â

The men each face seven charges, including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, that could land them decades in prison, if convicted. Soall was arrested in Spain in June, Hazan in Spain in August and Sheetrit in the U.K. in September. Their extradition requests are pending.

The indictment is the latest out of Manhattanâs federal court targeting nefarious use of AI. Earlier this year in the same court, a North Carolina man pleaded guilty to creating hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs and using bots to stream them, generating more than $8 million in fraudulent royalties. He was sentenced to 18 months in prison for one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

#7636. The midterms and SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the aftermath of Election Day, Republicans and Democrats alike are grappling with what the blue wave means for the Supreme Court. Keep reading to learn how the Senate shake-up, in particular, could affect when a justice next leaves the court and how the confirmation process might unfold.

Plus, one year ago today, the justices heard argument in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, a challenge to President Donald Trump’s tariff regime. Just over three months later, the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the president the authority to impose tariffs.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â Meta, Google and TikTok sued California over a new state law that prohibits certain social media platforms from using addictive features to target minor users.

The social media behemoths argued in three separately filed lawsuits Wednesday that the new regulations imposed by Assembly Bill 1709 violate the First Amendment by restricting the content they are allowed to show users under the age of 16.

The companies also argue the law is preempted by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields online businesses and social media platforms from liability for content posted by third parties.

âCalifornia Assembly Bill 1709 is Californiaâs latest attempt to flout that fundamental principle and appoint the state as the editor, curator, and controller of online speech,â Meta said in its complaint, filed in the Northern District of California.

Signed into law by California Governor Gavin Newsom on Sept. 10, Assembly Bill 1709 takes aim at âaddictive featuresâ such as algorithmic content recommendations, infinite scroll and autoplay. The bill prohibits social media platforms that use addictive feeds from allowing children under 16 to have accounts and creates an e-Safety Advisory Commission under the auspices of the state attorney general.

Meta argues the law would trample on the companyâs editorial judgment and that its choices about what third-party content to display on its platforms are protected by the First Amendment. Meta also claims that the contents of personalized feeds are protected third-party speech and the lawâs ban on autoplay would infringe on the companyâs right to engage in the âfree and unhampered distribution ofâ speech.

âWe are challenging this law because it violates the First Amendment by letting the government dictate how ideas are organized, displayed or shared with Californians,â a Meta spokesperson told Courthouse News. âUnder the law, we would be forced to either remove features that keep teens’ experiences age-appropriate, or cut thousands of California teens off from family, friends and their communities.â

In its lawsuit, filed in the Central District of California, TikTok claims the law would prevent it entirely from speaking to users under 16 through its current product, and would only allow the platform to engage with California users between the ages of 13 and 16 if it âdesign[ed] a fundamentally different offering.â

“AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use,â a TikTok spokesperson said.

âBeyond disregarding real progress in making teens safer online, this law limits free speech and takes away parentsâ rights to determine whatâs appropriate for their kids,â they said.

Google, the parent company of YouTube, similarly emphasized the need for parents to control their kids’ social media diet in its complaint filed in the Northern District of California.

The company argues that YouTubeâs personalized recommendations ensure that minor users receive relevant and appropriate content and that autoplay helps users consume content designed to be viewed âin a sequence.â

âWe believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,â a spokesperson for Google said.Â âOverly broad laws like this actually break the systems weâve built to help kids find high quality, age-appropriate videos.â

All three lawsuits name California Attorney General Rob Bonta as a defendant and ask the court to issue an injunction blocking Bonta from enforcing AB 1709.

A representative for the attorney generalâs office said they are reviewing the lawsuit and that their office is âcommitted to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.â

Meta, TikTok and Google are also challenging Senate Bill 976, also known as Californiaâs Protecting Our Kids from Social Media Addiction Act, which requires platforms to obtain verified parental consent before showing minors addictive feeds and to offer settings that let parents limit it.

In August, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila denied the social media companiesâ request for a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the statuteâs provisions. A few weeks later, the Barack Obama appointee rejected the platformsâ bid to keep the law from being enforced while they seek review in the Ninth Circuit.

#7631. Court to consider the reach of Article III courts in immigration contract dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem sure to get their focused attention: does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

Here, the Department of Labor, employing administrative law judges, for several decades has adjudicated disputes under the H-2A visa program, which allows employers to hire temporary foreign agricultural workers. The Department of Labor argues that Sun Valley Orchards failed in several ways to compensate such workers as it promised the government it would to qualify for the H-2A program. As is typical in such cases, administrative employees of the DOL (in its wage and hour division) charged Sun Valley with failing to live up to its obligations, and the DOL for the most part persuaded an ALJ that it was correct. On appeal, a different group of the DOL’s employees (its administrative review board) accepted the ALJ’s findings. At that point, for the first time, Sun Valley had a chance to take the dispute before Article III judges, but under the applicable statute the federal district court owes great deference to the DOL’s adjudication.

The case comes to the justices because the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit reasoned that the administrative adjudication of the department’s charges cannot be reconciled with Article III of the Constitution.

At a high level of generality, the doctrinal framework here is quite clear. All agree that Congress constitutionally can authorize adjudication by executive branch officials rather than judges, and all agree that its power to do so is limited to cases that involve “public rights,” a notoriously vague category designed to distinguish traditionally executive actions (like granting a visa) from disputes traditionally resolved in court (like tort and contract litigation). When those adjudications go beyond public rights, though, they infringe on the judiciary’s exclusive authority under Article III. The difficulty is that when you get down to details – defining the boundaries of “public rights” – the rulings have neither been stable nor persuasive. The point was made best by Chief Justice William Rehnquist (channeling Matthew Arnold), who famously characterized the decisions as “landmarks on a judicial ‘darkling plain’ where ignorant armies have clashed by night.”

For this particular dispute, the government contends that the case plainly involves public rights because it involves immigration or because it involves the assessment of remedies for transgression of privileges granted by the executive. By contrast, the employer characterizes the subject of the adjudication as a contract dispute. Granting the government’s free ability to decide (and adjudicate if it wishes to do so) the entitlement of any particular immigrants or group of immigrants to a visa or other immigration status, the dispute here involves whether the employer has complied with its employment contract. Because that is a prototypically private dispute – the kind of thing that could have been brought before a court at Westminster in Old England in the days of the drafting of Article III – the employer contends that it is not the kind of public right that Congress can have adjudicated by the executive.

It would be naïve to expect the justices will feel themselves constrained by the existing precedents on this topic. The case directly implicates the prerogatives of the judicial branch and the justices will see it that way. Moreover, decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a bench with a great appetite for reining in the administrative state even when precedents are settled and directly on point. And there is another problem for the government here – many of the cases they rely on predate the days of FDR and the rise of the administrative state. Furthermore, none of them crisply validates an administrative adjudication that takes money from one private party and gives it to another.

I would expect Justice Neil Gorsuch to be a major figure at the argument, as he has been pressing this particular point for several years, albeit in the context of the securities laws. For him, the government’s contention that the lower court decision would disrupt a large swath of long-accepted administrative arrangements will be a feature, not a bug. Chief Justice John Roberts also can be expected to be an important player, as he has written several of the modern opinions in the area. So this seemingly narrow dispute may herald something larger: yet another blow against the administrative state.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

Specifically, the state wants the federal court to narrow a challenged bill and sever any portions the court may find unconstitutional â such as those explicitly banning drag story hours â said Michael Noonan with the Montana Department of Justice.

âTo answer a question likely to arise: yes, we do not defend every word as written,â Noonan said. âThat is not a confession of judgment; it is an opening move of the narrowing case.â

The dispute centers on Montana House Bill 359, signed by Governor Greg Gianforte in 2023. The bill restricted drag performers from reading books to children and banned minors from attending what it described as âsexually oriented shows.â

Under the law, owners, mangers and employees of those shows would have faced fines from $1,000 to $10,000, and, for a third offense, would have lost their business licenses. Teachers and librarians could have their teaching or administrative certificates permanently revoked for a second violation. It also created a private right of action for aggrieved parents to sue those parties for up to 10 years.

A coalition of Montana businesses, nonprofits and performers who said the bill targets their First Amendment rights sued the state and in late 2023, U.S. District Judge Brian Morris ruled in their favor, preliminarily blocking enforcement of the bill.

This March, the Ninth Circuit upheld the injunction, finding the legislationâs restrictions are content-based limits on âpurely expressive activity.â

The plaintiffs and the state appeared before Morris, a Barack Obama appointee, again on Thursday with duelingmotions for summary judgment.

The state argued the plaintiffs donât have standing to challenge section two of the bill since it applies only to a âsexually oriented business,â which is defined as a ânightclub, bar, restaurant, or similar commercial enterpriseâ that serves alcohol and provides performances.

However, the plaintiffs contended that at least the Roxy Theater, a performing arts venue in Missoula, arguably falls within that definition.

âBars serve alcoholic beverages, restaurants serve food, nightclubs offer entertainment; the Roxy Theater does all three,â said Constance Van Kley, attorney representing the plaintiffs. âIf that isnât a similar commercial enterprise, I donât know what is.â

The state argued that while the theater serves alcohol, it is not a bar since alcohol isnât the primary source of its gross income.

The state also argued the court should adopt a narrowing construction and sever any portions of the bill it deems invalid.

âWeâre asking the court to apply the actâs own obscenity definition so the ban only reaches a performance that is obscene as to a minor and sever any remaining portions of the bill the court may find unconstitutional,â Noonan said.

But the plaintiffs argued federal courts canât issue a binding interpretation of state law and lack the power to interpret it in a way that revises the law.

âInstead, this is a question of âLetâs try to give effect to the legislatureâs intent,ââ Van Kley said.

Likewise, Morris seemed wary of altering the interpretation of the law.

âHow do I, looking back at what the Legislature did, fairly and accurately represent the views of those legislators in narrowing or changing the language of the statute?â Morris asked the state.

Montana argued the requested changes would work with what the legislature intended.

âWhich was, overall, keep certain performances away from minors that in this case would be obscene as applied to minors,â Noonan said.

The plaintiffs argued the statute is void for vagueness.

âWeâve spent three-and-a-half years talking about this statute and have not settled on a conclusive interpretation of it; I don’t know how an ordinary citizen or a law enforcement officer or a county attorney could do something weâre not able to do,â Van Kley said.

Morris questioned the state about the law’s limitations on parental consent.

âWhere do we draw the line here? Can a parent not consent to taking a child under this bill?â Morris asked.

Montana explained the state has an interest in shielding minors from explicit sexual content, much in the same way places like strip clubs have an age restriction.

Morris said he intends to return a decision before the end of the year.

The California Coastal Commission unanimously approved a massive beach armoring project to protect a vital rail corridor, despite years of criticism that the rocks and seawalls are eroding San Clementeâs public beaches.

(CN) â The California Coastal Commission voted unanimously on Thursday to approve a massive beach armoring project in San Clemente, California, in an effort to protect a valuable railroad line that runs along the coast that critics say comes at the expense of public beach access.

The permit allows the Orange County Transportation Authority, or OCTA, to retain and place about 50,000 tons of riprap, or large rocks, along the coast over the next 10-15 years to prevent the rail line from slipping into the ocean. It also includes the placement of 690,000 cubic yards of much-needed sand for beach nourishment and the construction of a seawall against part of the railroad.

The rail line in San Clemente has been increasingly threatened after recent storms in Southern California and the onset of Super El Nino.

Proponents of the project say it is necessary to protect the only railroad that links Los Angeles to San Diego, known as the LOSSAN Rail Corridor, that they say is vital to the regionâs economy and national security.

But critics of the permit describe the plan as the largest loss of public beach in the commissionâs history. They say that OCTAâs strategy of placing riprap along the beach has been irresponsible, shortsighted and ultimately a net negative for the rail corridor and the public.

Parts of San Clementeâs beaches have seen their width greatly reduced in the past decade, in some cases going from 200 feet in shore width to just 80, the commission staff said in its report on the permit.

Since 2021, the rail line has become increasingly vulnerable to coastal hazards, in part related to sea level rise and climate change, the commissionâs staff wrote. It has issued 15 similar track stabilization permits to OCTA and the Southern California Regional Rail Authority since then.

A few dozen residents and beach advocates expressed their disappointment during the meeting, held in San Francisco, that the continued approval of these permits has not helped anyone.

âThis is not a rail corridor,â Sarah Spinuzzi, legal director of the Orange County Coastkeeper, told commissioners.â©âIt is a community that has shaped California’s surf culture, home to the most prominent surfboard shapers around the world and the site of the 2028 Olympic surf venue.â

Spinuzzi was joined by a coalition that demanded guarantees from OCTA that it will maintain public beach access with a proactive approach and not just continue to armor the remaining beach.

Many public commenters asked for an amendment to OCTAâs permit to include a minimum of 50 feet of sandy beaches in front of the rocky revetments. Other groups, such as Save Our Beaches San Clemente, want to see an 80-foot minimum width of sandy beaches.

âOCTA has already destroyed Cypress Shore Beach and created impassable boulder piles where pristine beach once stood,â Lisa Gant, of Save Our Beaches San Clemente, told the commissioners. âPlease minimize the armoring footprint that OCTA is allowed to place on our beaches. Require OCTA to maintain a minimum sandy beach in front of their armoring. â¦ Require that they replenish that sand in a standardized schedule of monitoring and maintenance.â

Ocean waves scour the beach sand after the rocks are dumped, leaving less beach each year, said Save Our Beaches San Clemente President Suzie Whitelaw, who has a degree in marine sedimentology.

âThis process is inexorable,â she told the commission. âWeâre gonna be back here talking to you again and again and again for the next 10 years, and you’re gonna be seeing more and more rock and seawall added to our beaches, unless you do one simple thing, which is require them to maintain a wide, sandy beach in front of any armoring that they put in.â

Some commissioners found it difficult to approve a plan that had a long track record of failure.

âAlthough minimized, the impacts on public access and recreation are significant and unavoidable at this stage,â the commissionâs staff report said of the project.

Commissioner Susan Lowenberg, of San Francisco, described the transportation authorityâs plan as the definition of insanity. Other commissioners also expressed skepticism about OCTAâs proposal, given the history of beach armoring in San Clemente.

However, commissioners, officials and members of the public agreed that the sand nourishment proposal was much needed. Whether the proposed amount of sand was enough is not clear, commissioners and staff said.

The entire project might fall through if it wasnât approved today, Coastal Commission Executive Director Kate Huckelbridge said.

OCTAâs proposal is also contingent on $305 million in state and federal grant funding.

âI think doing nothing is never a good option, particularly in this case,â Commissioner Raymond Jackson, of Hermosa Beach, said. âThere’s no perfect solution. There is not even a good solution.â

Commissioners ultimately agreed to amend the permit to include a beach width assessment within five years of the project. The permit was approved, 11-0.

A spokesperson for OCTA did not respond to requests for comment.

MANASSAS, Va. (CN) â Naresh Bhatt shocked a Virginia courtroom Thursday when he testified that he had cut his wife’s body up after finding her dead from what he believed to be suicide.

Bhatt, 39, is on trial over the 2024 disappearance and presumptive murder of his wife Mamta Kafle Bhatt, 28. He has pleaded not guilty but admitted during testimony to charges of defiling a body and concealing a body. He maintains he did not kill his wife.

Mamta Bhatt’s family members and friends, wide-eyed, sat in a row behind prosecutors. Spectators in the packed courtroom gasped at his admissions, which contrasted with his previous claims he had no knowledge of his missing wifeâs whereabouts. Prosecutors say he previously gave shifting accounts of his wife’s whereabouts after her disappearance.

Mamta Bhatt’s remains have not been found, leading prosecutors to lean on circumstantial evidence such as an increase in their home’s water usage and Naresh Bhatt’s web searches.

During his second day on the stand, Naresh Bhatt said that on July 30, 2024, he discovered his wife unresponsive and next to a poisonous substance in a pool of vomit.

Bhatt said he attempted medical interventions himself, pulling the body into the bathroom and pouring water into his wife’s mouth. Instead of dialing 911, he said he panicked and decided to get rid of the body.

“Why didn’t you call literally anyone else for help?” asked Tracey Lenox, his attorney and chief public defender for Prince William County. “Were you concerned about how it would look?”

“I was concerned about everything,” he said.

Lenox then asked if he was afraid he would be blamed for driving her to suicide.

Prosecutors have characterized Naresh Bhatt as abusive. He testified Wednesday that his wife’s demeanor had changed in the months following the birth of their child.

Naresh Bhatt has maintained that he never physically abused his wife. During cross-examination, Deputy Commonwealthâs Attorney Matthew Sweet derided this, pointing out that Bhatt chopped her up.

“She loved you, always,” the prosecutor said.

Naresh Bhatt testified that after unsuccessfully trying to rouse his wife, he took his infant daughter to a babysitter’s house and returned home, where he considered hanging himself. Instead, he went to Home Depot, “to find anything to hide a body.”

He said he considered dumping his wife’s corpse in the Potomac River but then decided to chop the body up, “just to make it a smaller size so it fit in the can,” he said.

It was difficult. “I was trying to lower the body apart,” he testified. “Like, separate the legs from the body.”

Mentally and physically, he felt powerless, he added, explaining that initially, he did not have the strength to continue.

Later, he got back to work, partially using knives but primarily depending upon a saw, in which prosecutors claimed to have found blood.

Lenox asked if Naresh Bhatt finished cutting the body before neighborhood trash pickup came by, and if he knew the body would then be taken away. Naresh Bhatt answered affirmatively.

Bhatt said he did not throw his wife’s body in trash dumpsters around the area, as prosecutors contend. Instead, he only tossed out clothing and trash in the dumpsters, he said. While wiping his eyes on occasion, he mostly spoke without hesitation.

Mamta Bhatt was a nurse, and attendees included a contingent of nurses dressed in scrubs. When Sweet pointed to Bhatt and said, “You’re a liar,” and Bhatt responded, “yes,” applause rippled through the crowd.

#7624. Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On May 21, 2026, Justice Elena Kagan did something she had never done in nearly 16 years on the Supreme Court: she dissented alone in a signed decision. The case, Havana Docks v. Royal Caribbean Cruises, concerned whether cruise lines could face liability for using Cuban docks confiscated decades earlier. Eight justices, including Kagan’s liberal colleagues Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, sided against the cruise lines. Kagan thought the majority had misunderstood a basic principle of property law: the interest originally confiscated had expired long before the cruise ships arrived.

The solitary dissent was unusual for a justice who has spent much of her tenure avoiding separate opinions. At a judicial conference in July 2025, Kagan observed that the court “speaks best when it speaks as a court,” and acknowledged that she sometimes drafts dissents only to decide against publishing them.

Kagan’s professional background is also unusual. She is the only current justice who arrived at the Supreme Court without previously serving as a judge. Before her appointment in 2010, she had been a law professor, dean of Harvard Law School, a White House adviser, and solicitor general of the United States. Her career was therefore shaped substantially by institutions in which persuasion, negotiation, and managing competing perspectives are routine.

But how much does this explain her jurisprudence? Ideological measures generally place Kagan to the right of her liberal colleagues, and her voting record contains meaningful differences from Sotomayor’s and Jackson’s. Yet those differences are far from uniform, and Kagan’s reluctance to write separately persists even when she reaches precisely the same result as her colleagues.

Understanding Kagan therefore requires examining not only how she votes, but how she chooses to agree and disagree.

Kagan has generally occupied a position to the right of the other liberal justices in measures of Supreme Court ideology. But the distance between them depends considerably on how ideology is measured, which cases are examined, and when the comparison is made.

The best-known measure is the Martin–Quinn score, which estimates the justices’ ideological positions from their voting patterns over time. In the 2024-25 term, Kagan’s score was −1.85, compared with −2.80 for Jackson and −4.19 for Sotomayor. Kagan was thus the rightmost of the three liberals, although she remained substantially to the left of the court’s median justice, Amy Coney Barrett, whose score was +0.53. The estimates for Jackson and Kagan had been closer in earlier terms (and, in fact, Jackson was initially positioned slightly to Kagan’s right).

The scores capture something revealing about how the justices vote, but they do not directly measure the substance of their legal reasoning or their willingness to compromise. Nor does a justice’s location relative to the other liberals necessarily reveal whether her own jurisprudence has changed. Martin–Quinn estimates are relative positions derived from voting coalitions, and those coalitions are themselves influenced by the court’s membership and docket.

The voting record offers a more concrete comparison. During the 2010–2021 terms, there were 56 contested decisions in which Kagan joined the majority while Sotomayor dissented, compared with just 19 in which their positions were reversed. Kagan was nearly three times as likely to be on the prevailing side when the two disagreed. That is a substantial difference, although it does not establish that every disagreement reflected an ideological division.

Justice Stephen Breyer, long considered a moderate liberal on the court, provides a useful point of reference. During their overlapping time on the court, Kagan joined the majority without Breyer 41 times, while Breyer joined the majority without Kagan 31 times. The more balanced relationship suggests that Kagan’s historical voting behavior often resembled Breyer’s more closely than Sotomayor’s.

The picture has changed since Jackson joined the court in 2022. Across 121 contested decisions in which Kagan and Sotomayor both participated through the 2025 term, they voted on the same side 109 times. Kagan prevailed without Sotomayor seven times, while Sotomayor prevailed without Kagan five times. Their historical difference in majority participation has thus narrowed dramatically.

The convergence is particularly visible in closely divided cases. Of 82 decisions decided 5–4 or 6–3 in which Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson all participated, the three liberals voted together in 71. When the court divided most sharply, Kagan usually found herself alongside her liberal colleagues rather than occupying a position between the liberal and conservative wings.

There are then two different stories in the numbers. Over much of her tenure, Kagan was more likely than Sotomayor to support outcomes favored by conservative justices. More recently, that distinction has diminished, particularly in closely divided cases. Whether this reflects a change in Kagan’s jurisprudence or the changing opportunities for cross-ideological agreement remains uncertain.

The cases in which she breaks with her liberal colleagues offer a way to examine that distinction more closely.

One way to identify a comparatively moderate justice is to examine how frequently she votes with colleagues across the ideological divide. By that measure, Kagan has demonstrated considerable independence from her liberal colleagues.

Across 26 terms, Kagan was the only liberal voting alongside conservative justices in 27 contested decisions, approximately 5.3% of her non-unanimous votes. Sotomayor occupied that position in 18 decisions, or 3.4%. Yet Breyer did so in 29 cases, representing 7.1% of his contested votes during the years he served alongside Kagan. When he was on the court, Breyer, rather than Kagan, was more likely to separate from the other liberals in that way.

The pattern becomes even more interesting with Jackson’s arrival. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan was the sole liberal voting with conservatives in nine contested cases, compared with ten for Jackson (though this frequency has decreased) and just two for Sotomayor. Jackson’s cross-ideological votes were evenly divided between joining majorities and dissents, while Kagan’s predominantly placed her in the majority. Thus, even when two justices cross ideological lines with similar frequency, they may not be doing the same thing.

These voting coalitions also raise a question about Kagan’s reputation as a consensus-builder. Does she actually attract more conservative support when writing for the court?

The analysis provides surprisingly little evidence that she does. Of Kagan’s 47 majority opinions in contested decisions, 27 attracted at least three conservative votes. Sotomayor achieved the same result in 30 of her 49 contested majority opinions. Their records are then similar, suggesting that Kagan’s reputation for building agreement is not necessarily reflected in a distinctive ability to assemble ideologically diverse majorities.

The individual cases also complicate the idea that Kagan’s departures from the liberal wing are simply strategic compromises. In 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas, for example, Kagan wrote for six justices, including five conservatives, holding that the Constitution does not require states to recognize an insanity defense based on a defendant’s inability to distinguish right from wrong. Breyer, joined by Ginsburg and Sotomayor, dissented. Kagan emphasized the historical diversity of insanity rules and the latitude afforded to state legislatures; Breyer saw Kansas’s approach as eliminating a fundamental protection deeply rooted in criminal law.

Four years later, Pulsifer v. United States presented a dispute over the meaning of a single conjunction in a federal sentencing statute. Kagan wrote for a six-justice majority, including five conservatives, adopting a reading that restricted defendants’ eligibility for relief from mandatory minimum sentences. Gorsuch dissented, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, favoring an interpretation that would have made relief more widely available.

Neither case is easily explained as Kagan merely accommodating conservative colleagues and both show substantive disagreements over the meaning of legal rules, with significant consequences for criminal defendants.

These decisions also show why ideological distance and judicial method cannot be treated as interchangeable. Kagan’s cross-ideological votes sometimes reflect legal commitments that produce outcomes different from those favored by her liberal colleagues. They also suggest that her willingness to build agreement does not automatically lead her toward the narrowest available resolution.

If Kagan is not consistently more successful than Sotomayor at attracting conservative votes, the more distinctive feature of her jurisprudence may lie elsewhere: what she does after reaching agreement, and particularly when she decides that a disagreement warrants an opinion of her own.

The art of agreement: choosing when to write

The most distinctive feature of Kagan’s judicial behavior may have less to do with how she votes than with how she expresses agreement. During her 16 terms on the court, Kagan authored just 18 concurrences in signed decisions, compared with 81 for Sotomayor. Breyer, often described as an institutionally minded pragmatist, also wrote concurrences at more than twice Kagan’s rate during their overlapping service. Jackson has been considerably more prolific in her shorter tenure. Kagan’s comparative restraint is therefore striking even among justices who share many of her substantive positions.

The difference becomes even more revealing when the comparison is limited to cases in which the justices reached exactly the same outcome. Between 2010 and 2021, Kagan and Sotomayor both supported a conservative-authored majority opinion in 93 contested decisions. Sotomayor wrote separately in 13 of those cases; Kagan did so in just one. The difference is difficult to explain through ideology or case selection alone: the two justices were participating in the same decisions, agreeing with the same majorities, yet approaching the question of whether to write separately very differently.

The distinction has narrowed somewhat in recent years, but it has not vanished. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan wrote separately in three of 38 conservative-authored majorities she shared with Sotomayor, compared with five for Sotomayor. In 29 comparable cases involving Kagan and Jackson, Kagan wrote separately twice and Jackson eight times. These samples are smaller, but they reinforce the larger finding that Kagan is particularly reluctant to add her individual voice to an outcome she already supports.

Kagan herself has offered a remarkably candid explanation for this. Speaking at the 9th Circuit Judicial Conference in July 2025, she described the Supreme Court as an institution whose opinions should communicate a collective judgment. She acknowledged that producing a single institutional voice requires “a little bit of flexibility and compromise.” Separate opinions, she suggested, can complicate the law by presenting competing explanations of what the court has supposedly decided.

Yet Kagan’s restraint should not be mistaken for unqualified agreement. In 2024’s United States v. Rahimi, she joined Roberts’ majority upholding a federal restriction on firearm possession by individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders. She also joined Sotomayor’s concurrence, which defended the majority’s application of New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen while reiterating their disagreement with that earlier Second Amendment decision holding there to be a constitutional right to carry a firearm. Jackson wrote her own concurrence addressing the difficulties lower courts had encountered applying Bruen. All three liberals agreed with the outcome, but their choices about authorship differed.

A similar pattern appeared in 2023’s National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, in which the court rejected an argument by pork producers that a law violated the Constitution by regulating the pork industry outside of California. Kagan joined Sotomayor’s separate opinion explaining why they agreed with the judgment without embracing portions of Gorsuch’s reasoning that threatened to alter the established constitutional framework. Kagan was willing to register a qualification, but she did so by joining a colleague’s opinion rather than writing another.

These distinctions again complicate the portrayal of Kagan as a consensus-builder. The data do not show that she consistently attracts more conservative support to her own majority opinions than Sotomayor does. They show something different: Kagan is considerably more selective about articulating separate disagreements when she already supports the court’s disposition. That behavior may preserve a clearer institutional message, but it also leaves fewer public indication of her reservations about particular decisions.

The difference matters when interpreting Kagan’s ideological position. A justice who joins an opinion without writing separately may appear closer to its author than one who publishes a concurrence, even when both share the same substantive objection. Kagan’s record suggests the absence of a separate opinion can reflect a decision about judicial expression rather than any lack of disagreement.

The limits of agreement: textualism, precedent, and dissent

Kagan’s willingness to work across ideological lines has never meant avoiding deep disagreements with the court’s conservatives. Some of her sharpest opinions have challenged not only their conclusions but also their fidelity to the interpretive principles they profess to follow.

In a 2015 lecture at Harvard Law School honoring Antonin Scalia, Kagan famously remarked, “We’re all textualists now.” The observation acknowledged Scalia’s influence on statutory interpretation, including among justices who did not share his ideological commitments. Seven years later, in her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, Kagan explicitly revisited that statement: “It seems I was wrong.”

Her objection concerned the majority’s use of the major questions doctrine to restrict the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act. Kagan argued that the court had departed from ordinary statutory interpretation by demanding an unusually clear congressional authorization for agency action of substantial economic or political significance. In her account, the conservative majority’s claimed commitment to textualism yielded when the statutory text pointed toward an outcome it disfavored.

The exchange is revealing because Kagan was challenging the majority from within a methodology often associated with conservative jurisprudence. Her embrace of textualism did not entail agreement with the conservatives about what particular statutes meant, much less about how much authority courts should exercise over Congress and administrative agencies.

That distinction became even clearer in 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Writing for the three liberals, subject to Jackson’s recusal in one of the consolidated cases, Kagan defended Chevron deference (deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes) against the majority’s decision to overrule it. Her argument rested on statutory interpretation, congressional allocation of authority, administrative expertise, and the importance of precedent (a common theme for her). Textualism, in Kagan’s jurisprudence, does not necessarily require courts to resolve every statutory ambiguity without deference to an agency authorized to administer the law.

The same institutional concerns appear in her criticism of the court’s emergency docket. In Trump v. Wilcox, Kagan dissented from an order permitting the administration, pending further litigation, to remove officials from independent agencies. Joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, she objected both to the treatment of longstanding precedent and to the use of an expedited proceeding to alter the practical operation of existing law without ordinary briefing and argument.

These opinions provide an important counterweight to Kagan’s reputation for accommodation. Her restraint in writing separately does not preclude forceful disagreement when she believes the court has departed from established interpretive or institutional principles. Nor does that pattern necessarily distinguish her substantive positions from those of Sotomayor and Jackson, who joined these dissents.

The recurring question is therefore not simply whether Kagan is willing to compromise but where she draws the line between disagreements she can accommodate and those that she considers important enough to articulate publicly.

Sixteen years of decisions reveal a justice whose reputation for moderation captures only part of her judicial behavior. Kagan has historically been more willing than Sotomayor to join conservative-supported outcomes, and some of those differences reflect genuine disagreements about the law. Yet the gap has narrowed considerably in recent terms, particularly in cases that divide the court along ideological lines.

What distinguishes Kagan more consistently is her approach to disagreement. She is not uniquely successful at attracting conservative votes to her majority opinions. Rather, she is unusually reluctant to write separately when she can support an existing opinion, even in cases where her liberal colleagues reach the same result but feel compelled to explain their reservations. Her willingness to join another justice’s concurrence further complicates any assumption that silence necessarily signifies agreement.

The distinction has become more consequential as the court has moved rightward. Kagan’s opportunities to assemble majorities across ideological lines have diminished, while her dissents in disputes over administrative authority, precedent, and institutional power have become an increasingly public part of her jurisprudence.

Whether those patterns reflect a conscious strategy, enduring professional instincts, or some combination of the two cannot be determined from voting records alone. But the comparisons suggest that understanding Kagan requires looking beyond where she falls on an ideological scale. Her place on the court is defined both by the legal positions she takes and by the choices she makes about when – and how – to express them.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

#7623. Feds barred from pressing Washington state to toss voters’ ballots, for now

A federal judge found Justice Department prosecutors demanded, not requested, that Washington set aside roughly 400 votersâ ballots and threatened election officials who count them.

(CN) â Federal prosecutors can ask Washington state to set aside votersâ ballots, but they canât demand it, a federal judge in Seattle said Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead temporarily barred the Justice Department from pressing the state over a list of about 400 voters.

The Joe Biden appointee partially granted a request from OneAmerica Votes, the Latino Community Fund of Washington State and the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union, whose members include naturalized citizens.

On Oct. 26, eight days before Election Day, Acting U.S. Attorney Pete Serrano of the Eastern District of Washington and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd of the Western District sent Secretary of State Steve Hobbs the list. Mail ballots were already coming back to county offices.

They gave Hobbs 24 hours to review it and told him to have county election officials hold off on checking the signatures on those votersâ ballots, or counting them, until their “citizenship can be determined.â

At a press conference that day, Floyd warned that anyone who helps someone vote illegally âwould be also guilty of that crime under the aiding abetting theory.â

Hobbs refused two days later. Washingtonâs review found the list unreliable. At least 62 people on it hadnât been sent a ballot because their registrations were canceled, inactive or couldnât be found.

âWashington reviewed the list and found that it includes United States citizens â people who had already shown the state proof of their citizenship. Nothing in the record suggests that anyone on the list has been charged with a crime. The federal government has kept up the pressure anyway and has promised more lists and more letters,â Whitehead said.

Serrano said on the radio the next day that the department would turn to county auditors and could send “39 letters to 39 auditors over the next couple days.â He described the goal as making sure these ballots werenât counted.

The government told the judge it had taken no further action since the Oct. 26 letter. Whitehead disagreed.

âTheir own statements say otherwise,â he said.

The government argued the letter was only a request Washington was free to turn down, pointing to a recent Ninth Circuit ruling that put a nationwide order against similar demands on hold.

Whitehead said the distinction was between asking and compelling. The government, he said, âmay ask a state to set ballots aside, but it may not compel one to do so.â

âOn this record, defendants did not ask,â he said.

The Ninth Circuit ruled last week in a California case that a law criminalizing noncitizens voting in federal elections doesnât let the Justice Department âtake charge of or intervene in a stateâs administration of an ongoing election.â The Supreme Court declined to disturb that ruling Monday.

Whitehead found union members face a real risk of being discouraged from voting or having their ballots set aside. Only one plaintiff needed a legal right to sue, he said, so he didnât decide whether the other two groups have one.

âVoters who followed the rules should not lose their votes to a list that even its authors admit may include citizens,â he said.

The order applies to the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and four officials: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Serrano and Floyd.

They canât demand that any Washington election official remove specific voters from voter rolls, refuse them ballots or leave their ballots uncounted. They also canât threaten officials with criminal prosecution or investigation for refusing to comply.

The government can still investigate and prosecute people who vote illegally, share information with election officials, state its view of federal law and ask for cooperation. Whitehead did not order anything against President Donald Trump, who is also a defendant, and denied the governmentâs request to put the order on hold during an appeal.

The temporary restraining order lasts 14 days. Counties must certify results by Nov. 24. The government has until Nov. 12 to oppose a longer-lasting order, and Whitehead will hear arguments Nov. 18.

Representatives for the Justice Department and plaintiffsâ attorneys didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.

#7622. Cloud Platform Engineer at Supabase

As a Cloud Platform Engineer at Supabase, you’ll join Cloud Engineering, part of Engineering Operations, and shape the foundations that let engineering teams build, ship, and operate infrastructure safely and independently across AWS and GCP.

This is a role spanning cloud governance, platform engineering, and hands-on operations. You’ll work across AWS and GCP account structure, identity and access management, Infrastructure as Code (IaC), reusable platform primitives, security boundaries, and self-service workflows for engineers.

You’ll be joining at a point where many of these foundations are being actively defined or reworked. We’re looking for someone who can take ambiguous, messy, business-critical infrastructure problems and turn them into pragmatic systems, tools, standards, and written guidance that scale with the company and empower teams to go faster.

Designing and implementing cloud governance across AWS and GCP, including identity, account organization, access controls, and guardrails.

Building reusable infrastructure and building blocks using Infrastructure as Code (IaC), enabling teams to provision and manage infrastructure safely and consistently.

Creating self-service capabilities that reduce organizational friction and let engineers move more quickly within sensible boundaries.

Owning resource governance and visibility: management tagging, a trustworthy inventory of what exists and who owns it, and consistent cross-account billing data.

Developing reusable security primitives, including secrets storage, KMS, certificate management, token vending, direct service-to-service authentication, mTLS, and related platform services.

Owning cloud-level network and operational primitives: IP address management, DNS, and health signals such as service-limit and quota alerting.

Combining software engineering with hands-on operations and total ownership: building, deploying, monitoring, troubleshooting, and improving what you own.

Establishing and sharing cloud engineering best practices through documentation, internal tooling, examples, and enablement.

Have 5+ years of experience in cloud governance, platform engineering, and/or operations, have operated production systems at scale, and carried on-call for them.

Have previously undertaken a significant migration, e.g. rearchitected an AWS account topology, introduced IaC for existing infrastructure, centralized identity/SSO, or brought a second cloud under governance.

Enjoy building internal platform and self-service experiences for other engineers.

Are genuinely deep in at least one—ideally two—of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):

Tooling & ecosystem: You’re intimately familiar with the breadth of AWS services in general, and IAM/SSO in particular. You know their Well-Architected Framework, and when to reach outside. You have working knowledge of GCP. You use IaC routinely and have run it in production, whichever tool. You’ve probably collaborated with auditors on meeting compliance requirements.

Software engineering: You write real production code (Go, Rust, or a comparable systems language), and can build reliable, maintainable services. You thrive across all stages of the SDLC, set technical direction, know how to de-risk projects, and produce written artifacts such as RFCs.

Operations: You’ve run production infrastructure yourself: carried the pager, written the alerts and runbooks, used SLOs or similar to decide what to fix first, and made shared systems less risky over time. You like owning systems, simplifying complex infrastructure problems, and turning best practices into reusable building blocks.

Are comfortable treating infrastructure as software and have relevant experience with IaC and automation.

Communicate clearly, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

New remote jobs delivered to your inbox, every week.

Location independence is the future of work. It serves companies with best talent from around the globe. And benefits employees with a greater work life balance and the ability to work in their pyjamas.- Nithur, founder.
